templates.pattern: A community of [N_TOT] individuals contains species with counts: [N1], [N2], [N3], [N4], [N5]. Calculate Simpson's Index D = Σ[n(n−1)] / [N(N−1)]. Round to 4 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
Simpson's D = Σn(n−1) / N(N−1)
N = [N1]+[N2]+[N3]+[N4]+[N5]
= [RESULT]

This form of Simpson's D (dominance index) gives the probability that two randomly chosen individuals belong to the same species. Lower D = more diverse. The complementary index 1−D is used as a measure of diversity. The reciprocal 1/D indicates the effective number of equally-abundant species that would give the same diversity score.

templates.pattern: A community has [S] species with proportions p1=[P1]%, p2=[P2]%, p3=[P3]%, p4=[P4]%, p5=[P5]% (must sum to 100). Calculate Shannon's Diversity Index H = −Σ(pi × ln(pi)). Round to 4 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
Shannon H = −Σ(pi × ln pi)
= −(0.30×ln0.30 + 0.25×ln0.25 + 0.20×ln0.20 + 0.15×ln0.15 + 0.10×ln0.10)
= [RESULT]

Shannon's index combines species richness and evenness. Maximum H = ln(S) for perfectly even communities; H = 0 for single-species. The exponential e^H gives the 'effective number of species' (Hill number q=1). Typical values: tropical forests H=3–5; temperate grasslands H=1–3; agricultural monocultures H≈0.

templates.pattern: Using the species-area relationship S = c × A^z, where c = [C] and z = [Z] (expressed as z/100, e.g. 25 = 0.25), calculate the expected number of species on an island of area [A] km². Round to 1 decimal place.
templates.explanation:
Species-Area Relationship: S = c × A^z
= [C] × [A]^([Z]/100)
= [RESULT] species

The species-area relationship (SAR) is one of ecology's most robust empirical patterns. The exponent z typically ranges from 0.15–0.35 for oceanic islands and 0.10–0.20 for habitat patches. Halving habitat area reduces species by ~13% (z=0.25). SAR underpins habitat conservation targets — a 90% habitat loss predicts ~50% species loss. It is foundational to island biogeography theory (MacArthur & Wilson, 1967).

templates.pattern: Island biogeography theory predicts equilibrium species number S* = (I × E) / (I + E), where immigration rate I = [IMMIG] species/yr and extinction rate E = [EXTINCT] species/yr. Calculate S*. Round to 1 decimal place.
templates.explanation:
Equilibrium Species Number S* = I × E / (I + E)
= [IMMIG] × [EXTINCT] / ([IMMIG] + [EXTINCT])
= [RESULT] species

MacArthur and Wilson's dynamic equilibrium model (1967) predicts that species richness reaches a balance between immigration (decreasing as island fills) and extinction (increasing with more species competing). Larger islands have lower extinction rates; nearer islands have higher immigration rates. The model correctly predicted higher richness on large, near islands and inspired metapopulation theory.

templates.pattern: A continuous forest of [TOTAL_AREA] ha is fragmented into [N_PATCHES] equal patches. Calculate the area of each patch (ha) and the total edge length (m) assuming each patch is a square. (Edge length = 4 × √area per patch). Round area to 2 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
Patch Area = Total Area ÷ Number of Patches
= [TOTAL_AREA] ÷ [N_PATCHES]
= [RESULT] ha each

Fragmentation reduces patch size, increases edge-to-interior ratio, and isolates populations. Edge effects (altered microclimate, invasive species penetration, predation) can penetrate 100–300 m into fragments. A 100 ha square patch has only ~22 ha of core interior >100 m from the edge. Landscape connectivity — corridors, stepping stones, permeability of the matrix — can offset some fragmentation effects.

templates.pattern: Two habitat patches are [DIST] km apart. A wildlife corridor [WIDTH] m wide and [CORR_LEN] km long is proposed to connect them. Calculate the corridor area (ha). (1 ha = 10,000 m²)
templates.explanation:
Corridor Area = Width × Length ÷ 10,000
= [WIDTH] m × [CORR_LEN]×1,000 m ÷ 10,000
= [RESULT] ha

Wildlife corridors restore connectivity between fragmented habitats, allowing genetic exchange, recolonisation after local extinction, and climate-driven range shifts. Effective corridor width depends on the target species — carnivores need wider corridors (>1 km) than small mammals or invertebrates. The 'Y2Y' (Yellowstone to Yukon) corridor is one of the world's most ambitious connectivity projects, spanning 3,200 km.

templates.pattern: A population of [N0] individuals has an intrinsic growth rate r = [R_VAL] yr⁻¹ (express as decimal, e.g. 12 = 0.12). Demographic stochasticity causes the effective extinction time (years) to be approximated by Te = (2/r) × ln(N0). Round to 1 decimal place.
templates.explanation:
Extinction Time Te = (2/r) × ln(N₀)
= (2 / [R_VAL]/100) × ln([N0])
= [RESULT] years

Population viability analysis (PVA) estimates extinction risk through simulation of demographic and environmental stochasticity. Small populations face higher extinction probability even with positive growth rates, due to chance fluctuations. The 50/500 rule (Franklin, 1980) suggests 50 individuals to avoid inbreeding depression short-term, 500 for long-term evolutionary potential — now revised upward to 100/1,000.

templates.pattern: A breeding population has [N_MALES] males and [N_FEMALES] females. Calculate the effective population size Ne using Ne = (4 × Nm × Nf) / (Nm + Nf). Round to 1 decimal place.
templates.explanation:
Effective Population Size Ne = 4NmNf / (Nm + Nf)
= 4 × [N_MALES] × [N_FEMALES] / ([N_MALES] + [N_FEMALES])
= [RESULT]

Effective population size (Ne) is the size of an idealised population with the same rate of genetic drift as the actual population. Unequal sex ratios reduce Ne dramatically — a harem-based species with 1 male and 99 females has Ne = 4×1×99/100 = ~4, not 100. Other factors reducing Ne include fluctuating population size, variance in reproductive success, and overlapping generations. Ne/N ratios average ~0.1 across wild species.

templates.pattern: A captive breeding programme has an inbreeding coefficient F = [F_VAL]% for its stock animals. Inbreeding depression reduces fitness by a factor of (1 − [B] × F), where B = [B_VAL]. Calculate the relative fitness. (Use F and B as decimals, e.g. 20 = 0.20). Round to 2 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
Relative Fitness = 1 − B × F
= 1 − [B_VAL]/10 × [F_VAL]/100
= [RESULT]

Inbreeding depression occurs because inbreeding increases homozygosity, exposing deleterious recessive alleles. Studies show ~0.5–4% fitness loss per 1% increase in F in mammals. Zoo breeding programmes use studbooks and genetic algorithms (e.g., SPARKS software) to minimise mean kinship and F. Genetic rescue — introducing unrelated individuals — can dramatically reverse inbreeding depression, as demonstrated in Isle Royale wolves.

templates.pattern: A conservation triage ranks [N_SP] species by threat status and cost of intervention. A species scores [THREAT] out of 10 for threat level and [DISTINCT] out of 10 for evolutionary distinctiveness. Its intervention cost is £[COST] thousand. Calculate the conservation priority score = (Threat × Distinctiveness) / Cost. Round to 2 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
Priority Score = (Threat × Distinctiveness) ÷ Cost
= [THREAT] × [DISTINCT] ÷ [COST]
= [RESULT]

Conservation prioritisation frameworks (EDGE of Existence, IUCN Green Status, Zonation) balance threat level, ecological or evolutionary value, and feasibility. EDGE (Evolutionarily Distinct and Globally Endangered) scores combine IUCN status and phylogenetic uniqueness. Species high on EDGE lists include Pangolins, the Aye-aye, and the Bactrian Camel — flagging species ignored by charismatic megafauna-focused conservation.
